text: In many real projects the outcome you care about is rare. A few percent of transactions are fraud. A few percent of machines fail this month. Data like this is called imbalanced, and it quietly breaks habits that work on balanced data. This lesson shows how to spot it, why accuracy misleads, and which measurements to trust instead.

Start by measuring the imbalance. Run value counts on your target before anything else. In our illustrative dataset of five thousand rows, there are forty-seven hundred thirty-seven negatives and only two hundred sixty-three positives. That is about five percent, a ratio near eighteen to one.

Now the accuracy trap. Build a dummy baseline, a model that ignores every feature and always predicts the majority class. It scores ninety-four point seven percent accuracy while finding zero positives. The real logistic regression scores ninety-seven percent, only three points higher, yet it is the only one that catches anything. The dummy score is the number your model must beat.

So report the metrics that stay honest. Recall and precision for the rare class, separately. Average precision, which was zero point seven five five for our model. And a cost, when you know what errors cost. Notice recall is only forty-four percent. The accuracy hid that.

Here is the picture. On the left, the class counts: one bar towering over the other. On the right, the precision recall curve. The dashed line is random guessing, which sits at the positive rate, about five percent. The further the curve rises above that line, the more the model adds.

One more habit: always stratify. On a small slice with only eighteen positives, a plain random split sometimes left the test set with none at all. A stratified split kept four or five every time. Pass stratify equals y to train test split, and remember cross validation stratifies classifier folds for you when you give it an integer.
Up next, resampling: SMOTE and undersampling, and how to use them without leaking information.
